query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the in‐flight particle velocity by adjusting the HVAF‐i7 spray parameters (for example, reducing the spray distance to around 300–350 mm or modestly increasing torch power) will improve deposition efficiency and thereby enable the buildup of a thicker, adherent FeCoNiCrAl bond coat.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high‐entropy alloy powder with a particle size of 15–45 μm, which when sprayed with current HVAF‐i7 settings produces acceptable quality but insufficient coating thickness.
generation.intervention: Optimize the spray process to boost particle velocity – by operating at a closer, nozzle-specific spray distance (approximately 300–350 mm) and/or adjusting torch energy settings – to improve the kinetic energy of the particles during deposition.
generation.conditions: Deposition using the HVAF‐i7 torch under atmospheres and substrate geometries that include small internal diameters (~120 mm) and high-temperature service conditions typical of thermal-barrier applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The increased kinetic energy of the powder particles leads to more complete in-flight melting and improved splat formation upon impact, enhancing intersplat adhesion and reducing oxidation by shortening in-flight time.
generation.mechanism: Higher particle velocity improves the impact momentum, promoting better substrate bonding and layer buildup while reducing the time available for in-flight oxidation. This results in enhanced deposition efficiency and a thicker, denser bond coat.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (coatings produced with standard HVAF-i7 parameters), the adjusted spray parameters are expected to yield coatings with a significantly increased thickness while retaining acceptable oxidation levels and adhesion properties.
generation.baseline: Coatings from the HVAF-i7 torch using a 15–45 μm-feedstock under standard process parameters, which yield acceptable quality but inadequate thickness.
generation.boundary: The expected improvement is contingent on maintaining effective particle melting and substrate interaction; operating too close or with excessive energy might induce unwanted oxidation or splashing. The intervention should remain effective under typical deposition atmospheres and on substrates with internal diameters down to 120 mm, but extreme deviations in process conditions may compromise the results.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative gain in thickness and the optimal adjustments to particle velocity are not well defined and will require iterative experimental tuning. Additionally, scaling the intervention to complex substrate geometries may introduce additional fluid dynamic challenges.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeCoNiCrAl bond coats on identical substrates using the HVAF-i7 torch. One set will use the standard spray parameters (baseline) and the other will use the adjusted parameters designed to increase particle velocity (e.g., spray distance reduced to 300–350 mm and/or increased torch power).
measurements: Microstructural characterization (splat formation, porosity, and oxidation levels)
High-temperature performance tests (simulated thermal barrier service conditions)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings produced with the enhanced particle velocity intervention do not show a statistically significant increase in thickness compared to the baseline, or if they exhibit compromised adhesion or increased oxidation (deteriorating overall coating integrity), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The conventional principle of ESED is the generation of sparks when the anode and cathode come into contact, resulting in a very high local temperature that causes the anode electrode material to melt, transfer, and solidify onto the substrate. Similarly, when ESED is performed with powders, the powder particle in contact with the cathode substrate can be considered as the cathode during the powder deposition process. The high temperatures during the spark cause the powders to melt, fuse together, and solidify onto the substrate to form coating. In the ESPD process, when the electrode contacts with the dried powder slurry, the sparks are generated immediately. The slurry that has dark, rough, non-reflective surface starts burning, and transfer to a layer coating that has of silver, bright, and continuous surface.
